Every strategy has good periods and bad periods. A trend follower makes money when markets trend and bleeds when they chop. A mean reversion system does the opposite. So, the natural question is, can we detect which kind of market we're in and only trade when conditions favor our strategy? That's what market regime classification is about. We will start with the base concepts. So, what is a regime and the two dimensions that define it, then the indicators and the two families of classification methods, how to use regimes in practice, and then how to analyze the relationship between regimes and your trades, and how to validate the filter properly, and finally the Python notebook with all the calculations and backtests. A market regime is a period in which the market statistical behavior is relatively stable, similar volatility, similar tendency to trend or to revert. Every strategy is implicitly a bet on a regime. A breakout system, for example, assumes that moves tend to continue, while a mean reversion system assumes they don't. Knowing the regime means knowing when your strategy score assumption is likely to hold. We will describe regimes along two dimensions. The first is directionality. Is the market trending or is it moving back and forth around the mean? The second is volatility. How big are the moves regardless of direction? Crossing them gives us four quadrants, a quiet trend, a strong volatile trend, a calm range, and a choppy high volatile regime. Here comes an important asymmetry between the two. Volatility is persistent. High volatility days tend to be followed by high volatility days. You can see it in the auto correlation of absolute returns, which decays slowly. Direction is a different story. The auto correlation of returns is almost zero. So, today's volatility tells you a lot about tomorrow's volatility, but today's trend tell you much less about tomorrow's trend. In practice, volatility filters tend to be more robust than directional filters. To measure volatility, we have several options. First, the ATR, which is the classic indicator. Then we have realized volatility, which is just the rolling standard deviation of returns, GARCH, which models volatility explicitly and gives a conditional forecast, and for equity indices, implied volatility like the VIX. One important detail, don't use absolute threshold. Use a rolling percentile instead. It adapts to the market and generalizes much better. For directionality, the most famous indicator is the ADX, which measures trend strength. One I really like is also the Kaufman efficiency ratio, which is the net price change divided by the sum of all absolute moves. If price goes straight from A to B, the ratio is one. If it zigzags to get there, it's close to zero. Then there are statistical measures like the Hurst exponent, where values above 0.5 indicate trending behavior and below 0.5 mean reversion, and the variance ratio test, which compares variance over different horizons. Finally, we have the slope and R squared of a rolling linear regression. There are two main families of classification methods. Rule-based, you take your indicators and apply thresholds. It's transparent, easy to port, but every threshold is a parameter you're choosing. And then we have statistical methods like hidden Markov models or Gaussian mixtures, which learn the regimes directly from the data. They are more flexible, but the states they find need to be interpreted, and they hide a very common trap we will see in a moment. Regime classification is full of look-ahead bias. First, if you define high volatility as above the 70th percentile of the entire history, you're using future data. Use rolling or expanding windows. Second, using hidden Markov models, most libraries give you smoothed probabilities by default, which are computed using the whole series, including the future. So, if you look at the chart, the smoothed regime switches exactly at the turning points. It looks perfect because it's cheating. In a backtest, you must use the filtered probabilities, which only use the past data. And finally, indicators computed on the bar that hasn't closed yet. So, it works in the backtest, but in live it repaints. So, the rule is simple. The regime you use at time t must be computed with data up to t minus one. A filter is only useful if regimes last long enough. The transition matrix tells us the probability of moving from one regime to another. A strong diagonal means regimes are persistent, which is what we want. Then, compare the average regime duration with the lag of your indicators because if a regime lasts on average 20 bars and your indicator needs 15 bars to detect it, by the time you know where you are, the regime is almost over, so it's useless. Another practical problem. When the indicator hovers around the threshold, the regime flips every few bars and your strategy turns on and off continuously. So, this is a big problem. The two fixes are, first hysteresis, so use a higher threshold to enter and a lower one to exit. And secondly, use a minimum duration. So, the new regime must be confirmed for at least a certain number of bars, which is a small detail but makes a big difference on real results. Once you have a regime, there are four ways to use it. The obvious one is a binary filter, so you trade only in favorable regimes. But often, more robust is continuous position sizing. You scale exposure based on the volatility regime. Third, adapting parameters. Maybe in high volatility, you don't need to stop trading, you just need wider stops. And finally, at portfolio level, trend followers and mean reversion strategies prefer different regimes, so you can shift allocation between them. So, the matrix splits the market with thresholds which shows a priori, but we can also do better, so let the data tells us where thresholds should be. So, for each trade, we record the value of each indicator at entry and the outcome of the trade. Here is very important to normalize the outcome, so use the R multiple or P&amp;L divided by ATR. Otherwise, the volatility correlates with P&amp;L mechanically. The first idea is to compute a correlation coefficient, but the problem is that the relationships are often non-linear. A mean reversion strategy might work well at medium volatility and suffer at both extremes. That's an inverted U, and Pearson correlation gives you roughly zero, even though the relationship is very real. Spearman is more robust. Mutual information captures non-monotonic relationships. Even uh small correlation over hundreds of trades can still be economically meaningful. A much clearer approach is binned analysis. So, split the indicator into quintiles or deciles, and for each bin, compute expectancy, win rate, and a bootstrap confidence interval. Now, you see exactly why the strategy works and how uncertain the estimate is. You can also go in two dimensions, for example, using a heat map with one indicator on each axis and the expectancy as the color. This is the continuous version of our two-by-two matrix. It also shows interactions, which helps with a subtle problem, which is many indicators are correlated with each other, so you might attribute an effect on the wrong one. You can also look at the maximum, adverse, and favorable excursion. A regime might not change whether a trade is profitable, but could change how it gets there. So, for example, in high volatility, trades go deeper against you before working out. Data snooping is a problem with all these analyses, because if you test 10 indicators, five bins, and several strategies, something will look significant purely by chance. For example, this greed is random data and some beans still pass a 5% significance test. So, remember every threshold you pick is a parameter and filtering reduces the number of trades, so confidence intervals get wider, which brings us to validation. The minimum is an in-sample and out-of-sample split. You find thresholds in-sample and check that relationship on data you never seen before. First, keep the strategy fixed and validated separately and optimize only on the filter because if you optimize everything together, you don't know if the improvement comes from the strategy or the regime filter. And when you choose a threshold, pick the center of a plateau and not just the single highest peak. Even better is if you do a walk-forward analysis, but regime filters have a specific problem because regimes last months or years, so if your in-sample window is too short, it may contain a single regime and so the filter learns to exclude something it has never seen. So, windows must be long enough to include several regimes, which often means in using an in-cread or expanding walk-forward window instead of a rolling one. There are also two details. Indicator warm-up is better if you calculate it on the whole history, so you can access every value after the warm-up period. And also, I recommend plotting the thresholds selected in each window, so you can see if it jumps around, the filter is noise, basically. Any filter reduces the time in the market, so less exposure means lower drawdown and lower variance. The right benchmark in this case is to generate a thousand random filters with the same percentage of exposure and the same average regime duration and compute the metric for each. And if your filter doesn't sit clearly in the right tail of the distribution, it's not detecting anything. It's just trading less. So, the final comparison is made on the stitched out-of-sample segments. So, you have the unfilter strategy, the strategy with walk-forward filter, and the band of random filters. You can also add a the walk-forward efficiency to quantify the degradation from in-sample to out-of-sample. And finally, the holdout. So, a piece of data never touched during development, used once. Because if you rerun the walk-forward 10 times, trying different indicators, the walk-forward itself becomes in-sample. Now, let's move to the Python code. We will use the data from Yahoo Finance for the S&amp;P 500 from 2005 up to 2026 using an in-sample period up to 2015 and keeping a holdout set from 2023. We will calculate the rolling percentile over a year window, and we define a priori a threshold for the high volatility of 0.7 and for directionality of 0.55 with a hysteresis of a 0.10. So, the exit threshold will be 10% less than the entry, and for a number of confirmation bars equal to five. The strategies will have an ATR based stop-loss located three times the ATR from the entry. We will use two long-only strategies, which by the way are totally random. The first is a trend-following strategy based on a range breakout. So, we enter when the close breaks the 20-day high, and we exit when the close breaks the 10-day low. While the mean reversion strategy enters when the RSI 2 drops below 10 and exits when the close goes above the 5-day moving average. So, as a convention, we calculate the signals at the close of bar T, and then we enter and exit the trades at the open price of the next bar. We define the function for a basic backtester based on events, which requires the data frame with candle data, the vector of entries, and vector of exits, and the name of a strategy, which returns the trade table with all the statistics and the returns per bar of each strategy. So, as you can see here, this strategy copies the close, high, and low values from the data frame, and it defines both the trend and the mean reversion strategies giving the data frame and the entry and exit conditions. So, we run the backtests for both strategies and also for the benchmark, which is just buy and hold. And here we can compare the performance. So, the trend following has a sharp of 0.45 with 80 trades. The mean reversion strategy has 224 trades with a sharp of 0.34. And the buy and hold has a sharp of 0.43. Here we can see the comparison of the three equity curves. Here we can see that both strategies are not constant. So, what we want to do is, of course, try to detect certain regime profiles in these years so that we can just trade in these favorable market conditions. This is the series autocorrelation of both returns and absolute returns, which is a proxy for volatility. So, as you can see, for the volatility, there is a strong correlation of current returns from the past ones, which means that volatility is persistent, and it's very known in financial literature as volatility clustering, while returns are not at all so correlated except in this case for the bar at lag one, which is minus 0.10, which means that the S&amp;P 500 has a mean reversion component at lag one, which is also quite known. And in particular for returns, we have 13 values out of 40 out of the 95% bands, while for the absolute returns or volatility, we have all of them. Now, we define our main indicators. So, for volatility, we will use the realized volatility, which is the annualized rolling standard deviation of the last 20-day returns. Then, we have the ATR percentage, which is the ATR divided by the close price. For directionality, we will use the efficiency ratio by Kaufman, which is the net price change over the last 20 bars divided by the sum of the absolute daily changes. Then, we have the ADX, and finally, the variance ratio, which is the variance of 5-day returns divided by the five times the variance of daily returns over 120 bars. The variance ratio above one means positive autocorrelation, so trending, while below one means mean reverting. Here is a demonstration of the Kaufman efficiency ratio. So, in a straight line case, the ratio is 0.96. This is not a perfect line, so it's not one. While in a zigzag trend, the ratio is almost zero, in this case, 0.09. So, as we said, we will use not the absolute values of the indicators, but the position compared to the rolling percentiles. Here, you can see the realized volatility compared to the rolling 70 percentile, and we see the highlighted areas where the value is above the percentile. While here, we see the efficiency ratio and its rolling 55 percentile. We can plot the Spearman correlation matrix, and we can notice that realized volatility and ATR percentage are quite similar cuz they're basically the same thing. Also, we can see that ADX and efficiency ratio are somewhat correlated. And finally, we can see that efficiency ratio and volatility measures are negatively correlated because the more volatile a market is, the less efficient it is. So, now we use the thresholds we defined to split the market into four regimes and we get in total 35% of the time quite trend, 28% common range, 24% choppy or crisis and the 12% strong trend. Here we can see the market divided into each of the four regimes. So, we can zoom in and look at each one of them. Then for the statistical part, we will use the hidden Markov model, but since the HMM learn method predict proba returns smoothed probabilities, we have to create a custom function for getting the filtered version. These are the states the model finds fitted in sample. The low volatility regime has a positive daily mean percentage return and of course a low daily standard deviation, which is around 11% per year, while the high volatility regime has a negative daily mean percentage return and a much higher volatility. Both of them have a high probability to persist and the low volatility has an expected duration of 134 days, while the high volatility has a shorter duration of 42 days. Here we have both the Markov model filter and the rule-based high volatility state. So, the model is not binary, but has a probability of being in one regime or another, while the rule-based is either up or down. In this case, they agree on 75% of the data. In particular, the rule-based find 37% of the data to be in high volatility state. So, the first error we can make is the look-ahead bias, which in the rule-based filters using the whole sample for defining the thresholds, while using the hidden Markov models, he's using the smoothed probabilities instead of the filtered probabilities. Here we can see the two strategies, both in the unfiltered version and the filtered one, with and without the lookahead bias. And surprisingly, for the trend following, the lookahead version has a lower performance than the normal one, both for the rule version and the model version. While for the mean reversion, only the rule version is better than the lookahead version. So, this tells us that not necessarily knowing the right regime in advance gives us an advantage. We can compare both the smoothed and filtered Markov models on the 2008 crisis. The smoothed version is much more faster responding to the regime change, and on average, the filtered version has a two-day delay compared to the other one, which looks like a small difference, but it can make a big difference because if every time you have this two days delay, you skip very bad trades, the performance over the whole period will be much different. Given our data, we can compute the transition matrix from one regime to the other. All four regimes are very persistent, so the probability of having the same regime tomorrow is above 90%. We can also see the distribution of the regime durations. In particular, the quiet trend has a duration of 21 bars, the strong trend of 11, the calm range of 15, and the choppy of 18. This duration is very important because it needs to be compared to the indicator lag, cuz if the indicator is too slow in detecting the regime, it's worthless cuz once you detected a new regime, it's already ended. If we calculated the lag of each indicator, the volatility indicators are quite fast compared to the regimes they detect. So, only about 20% are shorter than the lag, which is good. While for the directional indicators, the lag is much higher and around 60% is shorter than the lag. So, this is a big problem because this means that most time they detect a regime that it's already ended. A second problem we have is with whipsaws, which is when the indicator oscillates continuously around the entry threshold and we can remedy that using first the hysteresis, so having a higher threshold for entry and a lower threshold for exit. And furthermore, by using a number of days of confirmation before triggering the new regime, which further consolidates the new state. And in particular, we can see for volatility regimes, using the hysteresis decreases the switches from 160 to 95 and adding also the minimum duration to 69. While for directional regimes, which is triggered continuously, as you can see, the hysteresis reduces by 100, while the minimum duration decreases significantly to 200. And this also increases quite a lot the mean duration of each regime, which is also very important. Now, we calculate the expectancy of each strategy by regime on the in-sample period. And as you can expect, the trend follower strategy performs really well in a strong trend, but also in a counter range regime, while the mean reversion strategy performs better, surprisingly, in the quiet trend and strong trend. But, also consider that for the trend following strategy, we have a very low number of trades, so this is not too reliable as an estimate. For the mean reversion, we have more trades. Here you can see that in both the quiet trend and the strong trend, the win rate is quite high with a positive R, while in a counter range and choppy regime, we have both a lower win rate and a negative R, which means the payoff ratio is much lower. Once we detect the regime, we can use it both as a binary filter to trade or not to trade, or by varying our volatility targeting. And we can see that applied for both strategies here. For the trend following strategy, the binary filter works better than the volatility targeting, while for the mean reversion strategy, the volatility targeting works better than the binary filter. Also notice that the Sharpe ratio increases compared to the unfiltered version. In particular, the exposure is almost the half, keeping the total return about the same. And also the drawdown is cut from 27% to 8%. Also, in the mean reversion strategy, the drawdown is less than half, but in this case, the total return is lower as well. Over then defining thresholds a priori, we can also study the relationships between the indicators at the entry moment and the trade outcome. Here you can see a synthetic inverted U, where the Pearson correlation would return zero. Here we have the trend follower strategy and mean reversion. In the trend follower, we can see, even though we have a low number of trades, that the strategy performs at best in the mid range of volatility, while for the mean reversion strategy, it's not so clear. The only two relevant relationships are between the variance ratio in the trend following strategy and the ADX in the mean reversion strategy, but no one appears like the synthetic data. So, these are all weak relationships. Another analysis we can do is to split each indicator into quintiles and the plot each bin against the expectancy. So, we can see for the trend following strategy, the best expectancy is for the mid-range volatility, as we saw before, and for higher values of the efficiency ratio. So, more efficient markets tend to perform better in trend following, while for the mean reversion, it prefers lower volatility and a higher efficiency ratio. Also, the fact that a strategy has a positive expectancy in multiple bins and also having a flat region tells us that the strategy can perform well in different conditions for data regime, while having just one large bin and all the others flat or zero is telling us that the strategy is not performing well in these conditions. For the trend following strategy, for mid values of volatility, where we have positive expectancy, we also have a high win rate. While for higher volatility, we have a very low win rate. Also, for the case of efficiency ratio, we can see that for increasing values, the win rate increases quite a lot, and so does the mean R. For the mean reversion strategy, the win rate is more stable, but the mean R changes as we saw before. This is the same information, but using two-dimensional heat maps. So, the trend follower works better in high efficiency markets and mid to volatility, while mean reversion works well under all three ranges of efficiency, but on mid-to-low volatility. This is very useful because you can see the interconnections between different regimes combinations. We can also look at the performance in terms of maximum adverse excursion and maximum favorable excursion. In this case, the adverse one is almost the same between low and high volatility for both strategies, but what changes is the favorable excursion, especially for the trend following strategy, goes from 0.81 to 1.12 and from 0.27 to 0.35 in the mean reversion. Also, the share of trades stopped in the low volatility are half the ones in high volatility for the trend following strategy. The third problem we can have is data snooping bias. So, by testing so many combinations, the probability of having a relevant bin for luck is much higher. Testing of random data using several indicators and bins, so we have grids of 50 and we find a rate of false positives per grid of 2.5. We find seven bins out of 50 marked as relevant at 5% level. So, in our particular case, we found in total five bins marked as relevant against 2.5 out of 50 tests we made. But, consider that these bins are not independent of each other because, first of all, they are all from trend following, which has a low number of trades. Three of them are from realized volatility, which is also very correlated with ATR. The only one very distant from multiple testing is this last one with a P value of 0.001. So, now we want to validate our findings out of sample. So, we keep our strategy parameter fixed, then we fine-tune the thresholds for each indicator in sample using Sharpe ratio of daily returns as the metric and try to optimizing on plateaus and not peaks. We use the in-sample period we defined in the beginning, so from 2006 to 2015 and the out of sample from 2015 to 2023. While in this case, we are more distant from the optimal out of sample performance, but as you can see, if we just optimize on the in-sample, the curve is quite oscillating, so probably much of this is just noise and it's much better to smooth the curve and just optimize on the highest value here. For this last indicator, we choose the highest one, but ultimately out of sample, almost all the values perform poorly, so we can do much about that. What we find in this table is that the out of sample Sharpe using the plateau method is higher than the peak method just for the mean reversion strategy. It's almost identical for the trend following strategy, but also what we can see is that the out of sample Sharpe in the trend following is always inferior to the unfiltered out of sample, Well, for the mean reversion strategy, we find that realized volatility and ATR produce much higher Sharpe ratios than the unfiltered version. Then we can also run an incredible walk forward on filter to check for the threshold stability. So, instead of using rolling windows, we use always the same start. If you look at the results, the thresholds are quite stable throughout the years, except from the ER for the trend following, which changes sign, and also the ADX for the mean reversion strategy, both in the last year, and especially the variance ratio, which changes quite a lot. Now, since all filters reduce market exposure and so max drawdown, we want to compare our filter with a certain number of random filters having the same average exposure to the market and the same regime duration to check if the timing of our regimes actually matters. So, for each walk forward filter, we generate 1,000 random filters using a Markov chain, and we compare the results of the random filter with our real filter, and we expect our to be on the right tail of the distribution. This is the median result we obtain with the random filter for the trend following strategy. All results are better than the filtered. A percentage is between 6 and 25 are better than the random filter. While for the mean reversion strategy, the median is much lower, and since we got high values for the volatility indicators, we find that 95% and 100% of our filters beat the random ones. While for directional indicators, just 60 for the efficiency ratio and about 30% for the other indicators. Here you can see the histograms of all the tests we made, and it's evident how the only relevant tests are the realized volatility and ATR for the mean reversion strategies because all the others lie on the left side of the histogram. Here you can see the walk forward equity. So, for the trend following strategy, both filters reduce the exposure and the drawdown, but they also reduce the opportunities to grow. While for the mean reversion strategy, clearly the volatility filter adds value to the strategy also in comparison to random filters. While the directional filter smooths the equity curve a little bit, but it's not so much better compared to other random filters. Finally, we test the filters we found so far on our last piece of data we never touched before. So, this set is from 2023 to 2026, and this is the result. So, for the trend following strategy, the filtered version has a lower performance in every case compared to the unfiltered version. While for the mean reversion strategy, only the realized volatility has a greater performance, while the ATR percentage is lower. And the efficiency ratio, which in the previous test was failing, in this case it gives a higher performance than the unfiltered one. And so also does the variance ratio. So, this is a weak proof that in this case the volatility adds value to the strategy. And so this means that neither filter is strongly confirmed in this test. So, to recap, the regime is defined by directionality and volatility, and volatility is the more predictable of the two. Classification hides a lot of the look ahead bias, rolling thresholds, filtered probabilities, close bars. To find where your strategy works, analyze trade by beans and heat maps, not just correlation coefficients, and validate everything. Walk forward, hold out, and the random filter benchmark.
